Each question is worth 1 point. Circle one answer for each.

## Question 1 (1 point)

A bootstrap SE for a sample of $n = 30$ observations is computed from
$B = 1000$ bootstrap samples. What changes if $B$ is raised to $100{,}000$?

1. The bootstrap SE converges to the true SE of $T$.
1. Both the Monte Carlo error and the error from using $\hat F$ in place of
   $F$ shrink.
1. The Monte Carlo error shrinks, but the error from using $\hat F$ in place
   of $F$ does not.
1. Nothing, because every one of the $30^{30}$ possible bootstrap samples
   is already drawn.

### Solution

**Answer: 3.** $B$ controls only how well the $T^*_b$ describe the bootstrap
distribution, which is the sampling distribution of $T$ under $\hat F$. That
distribution differs from the one under $F$ no matter how large $B$ is, so
option 1 and option 2 are wrong. Option 4 is wrong because
$30^{30} \approx 2 \times 10^{44}$, far more than 1000.

## Question 2 (1 point)

When would you use a basic or percentile interval instead of the normal
interval, $T \pm z_{1 - \alpha/2} \, \widehat{\text{SE}}$?

1. When the bootstrap distribution of $T^*$ is skewed.
1. When $B$ is small, because quantiles need fewer bootstrap samples than an
   SE.
1. When $T$ is the mean of a large sample.
1. When the bootstrap SE is large.

### Solution

**Answer: 1.** The normal interval uses only the SE, so it is symmetric about
$T$ and assumes $T$ is approximately normal. The basic and percentile
intervals use quantiles of the bootstrap distribution, so they can reach
further on one side, as for the Flint 90th percentile without the two
excluded samples. Option 2 is backwards: tail quantiles need a larger $B$
than an SE does. Option 3 is the case where the normal interval works well.
Option 4 is wrong because a wide symmetric distribution is still fit by the
normal interval.

## Question 3 (1 point)

Each of `n` homes has a first-draw lead level `x[k]` and a level after
flushing `y[k]`. Which code computes one bootstrap replicate of the mean
difference of logs?

1. `mean(log(sample(x, replace = TRUE)) - log(sample(y, replace = TRUE)))`
1. `i <- sample(n); mean(log(x[i]) - log(y[i]))`
1. `i <- sample(n, replace = TRUE); mean(log(x[i])) - mean(log(y))`
1. `i <- sample(n, replace = TRUE); mean(log(x[i]) - log(y[i]))`

### Solution

**Answer: 4.** $\hat F$ puts mass $1/n$ on each pair, so resample rows and
keep each home's two values together. Option 1 resamples the columns
separately and breaks the pairing. Option 2 samples without replacement,
which only reorders the homes and returns the observed mean every time.
Option 3 resamples `x` but not `y`.

## Question 4 (1 point)

For which of these statistics would the bootstrap **not** give a good
estimate of the sampling distribution?

1. The sample correlation.
1. The sample maximum.
1. The sample median.
1. The mean difference of paired observations.

### Solution

**Answer: 2.** A bootstrap sample can only reuse observed values, so $T^*$ is
never larger than the observed maximum, while the true maximum can be. The
bootstrap needs a small change in $F$ to make a small change in $T$. The
correlation and the mean difference are smooth functions of means, so they
work well. The median and other quantiles work roughly, as the Flint 90th
percentile did.

**Rubric.** 1 pt per question, no partial credit.
